content: To improve supply chain management in healthcare, strategies should be tailored to local needs. This includes creating protocols for acquiring and maintaining an adequate stock of supplies. Implementation strategies must be adapted to fit within the constraints of existing systems. Providing appropriate incentives can encourage the recording of necessary information. It is also important to explain to target users the reasons behind conflicting recommendations and to educate them on the benefits of adhering to recommended practices. The impact of implementing guidelines and recommendations can be monitored at health service, regional, and national levels using clearly defined criteria and indicators aligned with locally agreed targets. Data collection at country and regional levels, in collaboration with WHO monitoring and evaluation teams, will assess the impact of these recommendations on national policies in WHO Member States. Research implications highlight the need for further studies in areas where evidence is uncertain or limited. This includes interventions assessed in single studies, those requiring replication in different settings, and predefined guideline questions that lack sufficient research. Future intervention trials should be preceded by formative research to identify locally relevant factors influencing cesarean births. Research should focus on healthy women seeking antenatal, labor, and delivery care in various settings, particularly in areas with high or increasing cesarean section rates. Pragmatic randomized controlled trials or cluster-randomized trials are recommended, and where these are not feasible, interrupted time series designs should be used. Studies should be adequately powered to assess primary and secondary outcomes and consider factors such as parity, socioeconomic status, staffing patterns, and geographical region. Multi-site and mixed-methods studies are encouraged to enhance generalizability and provide insights into intervention effects. Interventions should be multifaceted and tailored to local determinants of cesarean section practices. Educational interventions for women, such as birth preparation classes, telephone psychoeducation, and prenatal education for partners, should be explored. For healthcare professionals, audit and feedback using the Robson classification are recommended. Organizational interventions, such as insurance reforms equalizing physician fees for vaginal and cesarean births and collaborative midwifery-obstetrician care models, should also be considered. Additional research is needed to confirm the benefits of interventions like midwife-led continuity models, continuous intrapartum support, simulation-based training, and physical activity-based interventions. The WHO guidelines will be disseminated through online and print versions, translated into multiple languages, and shared with stakeholders, including ministries of health, professional associations, and non-governmental partners. Policy briefs summarizing recommendations and implementation issues will be developed for policymakers and program managers. The guidelines will be updated regularly based on new evidence, ongoing studies, and feedback from technical experts and healthcare professionals. WHO will continue to monitor research developments and assess the need for new or updated guidance. All technical products developed during the guideline process will be archived for future reference.
